channel.title: Pi Stack
channel.description: Comprehensive guides for open source alternatives, self-hosted software, privacy tools, and local AI deployment. Expert comparisons, setup guides, and benchmarks.

item.title: Postgres in the Browser in 2026: PGlite vs libSQL/Turso vs postgres-wasm
item.description: Your users are on a train with two bars of signal, and your app still has to answer a query in under 50 milliseconds. Round-tripping to a Postgres instance in us-east-1 is not going to do it. That is the problem embedded databases solve — and in 2026 the options finally got good enough to ship.

item.title: Stop Running Redis Just for Background Jobs: Graphile Worker vs pgmq vs River in 2026
item.description: Every architecture diagram starts the same way: one Postgres box and good intentions. Then somebody needs a nightly invoice run, and suddenly there is a Redis instance, a Celery worker pool, a Flower dashboard, and a second on-call rotation for a cache server that is now load-bearing.

item.title: TypeDoc vs API Extractor vs JSDoc in 2026: Which One Actually Generates Docs Developers Read?
item.description: Every TypeScript library has the same three-week window: the code is clean, the README is honest, and nobody has published API docs yet. Then the first external contributor opens an issue asking what an options object actually accepts, and you realize the types are the documentation — except nobody can browse a .d.ts file comfortably.

item.title: Duende vs OpenIddict vs ASP.NET Core Identity in 2026: Pick the Wrong One and You'll Rewrite Auth Twice
item.description: Every .NET team builds the same thing twice. First they add a login form, a User table, and a JWT — done in a weekend. Eighteen months later a partner needs SSO, a mobile app needs refresh tokens, a second service needs to validate tokens, and someone asks for “Sign in with Microsoft”. That is when the weekend decision becomes an architecture problem.

item.title: Go Dependency Injection in 2026: Wire vs Dig vs Fx — Compile-Time, Runtime, or Framework?
item.description: Go’s standard advice used to be “you don’t need dependency injection, just pass the struct.” Then the service grew to forty constructors, main.go became a hand-written wiring diagram eleven screens long, and every new handler needed three edits in three files. That is the moment teams reach for a DI library — and immediately disagree about which one.

item.title: kotlinx-datetime vs ThreeTenABP vs java.time in 2026: The Kotlin Date Trap Nobody Documents
item.description: Here is a bug that ships to production more often than any other in Kotlin: a meeting scheduled for 9:00 tomorrow shows up at 8:00 or 10:00 for half your users. Nothing crashed, no test failed, and the code looked correct. Someone stored a LocalDateTime and later converted it to an instant using the server’s zone.

item.title: Phoenix LiveView vs Laravel Livewire vs Hotwire Turbo in 2026: Which Server-Rendered UI Stack Wins?
item.description: Single-page apps promised snappy interfaces and delivered a second backend: a JSON API, a state store, a router, and a build pipeline to keep them in sync. By 2026 a lot of teams have quietly walked that back — not to jQuery-style spaghetti, but to a third model where the server renders HTML and pushes updates over a socket, and the browser holds almost no application state.

item.title: PHP GraphQL in 2026: webonyx/graphql-php vs Lighthouse vs GraphQLite — Which Should You Ship?
item.description: REST endpoints multiply like rabbits. You add /orders, then /orders/{id}, then /orders/{id}/items, then a mobile client asks for a trimmed payload and you bolt on ?fields= — and three months later your API surface is 40 routes nobody can document. That is exactly the wall where PHP teams start typing composer require something with “graphql” in the name.

item.title: Ruby GraphQL in 2026: graphql-ruby vs graphql-batch vs graphql-guard — Which One Do You Actually Need?
item.description: Your GraphQL endpoint returns 200 OK in 40 ms locally. In production it takes 2.3 seconds, and the database log shows the same SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id = $1 repeated 340 times in a single request. Nothing is broken — you just shipped a graph without a batching layer, and every nested field fired its own query.

item.title: Carbon vs Chronos vs Brick\DateTime in 2026: Which PHP Date Library Should You Actually Use?
item.description: Every PHP team eventually ships a billing bug that only reproduces twice a year. Mine was an invoice that landed on the wrong day for users in Santiago: the job ran at 00:30 local time, the server stored UTC, Chile shifted its offset, and strtotime('+1 day') cheerfully produced a timestamp 23 hours later. The fix was not a cleverer string function — it was replacing the ad-hoc date handling with a library that models time zones as first-class data.

item.title: Clojure Database Libraries in 2026: next.jdbc vs HoneySQL vs HugSQL
item.description: You have a Clojure service, a Postgres database, and three libraries that all claim to be “the SQL layer.” Pick wrong and you will spend the next two years writing (first (jdbc/query ...)) wrappers around a wrapper — or worse, string-concatenating user input into a WHERE clause.

item.title: Odin vs C3 vs V in 2026: Three Modern C Alternatives Compared With Real Code
item.description: You have a 40,000-line C codebase, a build that takes eleven minutes, and a static analyzer that gives up somewhere around the third macro expansion. Rewriting in Rust is a two-year project nobody will fund. So you look at the three languages that promise C’s mental model without C’s foot-guns — and immediately hit the real question: Odin, C3, or V?

item.title: PHP Image Processing in 2026: Intervention Image vs Glide vs Imagine
item.description: Resize a 12-megapixel JPEG on every page view and your PHP-FPM worker spends 200–400 ms and roughly 40 MB of RAM per request doing it. Ten concurrent visitors and you have allocated half a gigabyte to produce ten identical thumbnails. That is the moment you start caring about which PHP image library you picked — and by then it is usually welded into 40 controllers.

item.title: Prawn vs HexaPDF vs CombinePDF in 2026: Which Ruby PDF Library Should You Actually Use?
item.description: A Ruby PDF bug rarely looks like a PDF bug. It looks like a Sidekiq worker that balloons to 1.8 GB of RSS on a 900-page statement run, or an invoice attachment that renders beautifully in Preview and as blank pages in a bank’s document portal. Ruby has three mature ways to produce PDFs and they solve genuinely different problems: Prawn draws documents, HexaPDF reads and rewrites them, and CombinePDF stitches existing pages together.

item.title: Ruby Authentication in 2026: Devise vs Rodauth vs Sorcery — Which One Actually Fits?
item.description: Devise has 24,356 GitHub stars and shows up in essentially every Rails tutorial, which is exactly why so many teams install it without asking what they bought. What they bought is ten modules compiled into one model — database_authenticatable, registerable, recoverable, rememberable, trackable, validatable, confirmable, lockable, timeoutable, omniauthable — most of which they will never configure correctly, and two of which shipped security advisories in 2026.

item.title: Go Compression Libraries in 2026: klauspost/compress vs LZ4 vs DataDog/zstd
item.description: Every Go service that writes JSON to Kafka, ships logs to a collector, or caches a 4 MB response eventually hits the same wall: compress/gzip burns an entire core on the hot path. The standard library is safe, stable and slow — roughly 3× slower than the best third-party option at the same compression ratio, according to the benchmarks published in klauspost/compress. Swapping it out is usually a one-line change, but the three popular replacements have very different costs hiding behind that line.

item.title: Go Internationalization in 2026: go-i18n vs gotext vs golang.org/x/text
item.description: Adding a second language to a Go service looks like a two-hour task until you hit plural rules. English has two forms, Polish has four, Arabic has six, and Japanese has one — and the moment a product manager asks for “3 pliki” versus “5 plików” you discover that fmt.Sprintf with an if count == 1 branch is not an internationalization strategy. Go has no blessed answer in the standard library; there are three credible packages and they disagree about almost everything: message format, translation workflow, and who owns plural logic.

item.title: Go Terminal Styling in 2026: Lipgloss vs fatih/color vs Aurora
item.description: Your Go CLI prints grey text on a black background, and users assume it is a toy. That single aesthetic decision costs you adoption before anyone reads your --help output. Terminal styling is not decoration — it is how a CLI signals which line is an error, which row is selected, and where the eye should land first.

item.title: Ruby Recurring Jobs in 2026: rufus-scheduler vs Whenever vs GoodJob vs sidekiq-cron
item.description: You add one line — every 1.day, at: '4:30 am' — and ship it. Three weeks later the nightly invoice job has run twice on Tuesdays, not at all on the day you deployed at 04:29, and nobody can tell you which of the four Rails hosts actually executed it. Recurring jobs are the smallest feature in your app with the largest blast radius, because the failure mode is silent and the damage is already written to the database by the time anyone notices.

item.title: Rust Compression Crates in 2026: flate2 vs zstd vs brotli vs snap
item.description: A single zstd dependency can cut your archive size by more than half and still run faster than gzip — but only if you picked the right crate, at the right level, for the right payload. Most Rust codebases pick their compression crate by copying whatever their HTTP framework already depended on, then wonder why a 40 GB log partition fills up in eleven days.
